lessons.title: Send a value across a process boundary
lessons.explanation: An object reference identifies an object within its process. To call a remote component, Binder carries a marshalled representation of arguments. The receiver can reconstruct values in its own memory. A Binder interface handle is a special case that enables later calls across the boundary.
lessons.example: Process A sends a parcel containing a note title equal to River. Process B decodes the title and renames its local note to Lake. A still reads River unless B sends a result or both consult shared durable storage.
lessons.exercise: A callback needs to notify A when the edit completes. Would sending the original Java object address establish that callback?
lessons.answer: No. Pass a supported Binder interface or another explicit reply mechanism. The remote process cannot dereference A’s object address.

lessons.title: Pass an identity through an Intent
lessons.explanation: An Intent describes the work to perform and can carry named extras. A screen opened by another component needs an explicit contract for names, types and missing values. Passing a small stable record ID also lets the destination load the current record after recreation.
lessons.example: The list adds putExtra("note_id", 17L). Detail reads a long with a reserved fallback, checks that the ID is valid and loads note 17. If it no longer exists, detail shows a missing-note state.
lessons.exercise: Why is passing a 12 MB photo in the same extra a poor replacement for passing the ID?
lessons.answer: Interprocess transactions have bounded buffer space and the image adds copying and lifetime problems. Pass a content reference with appropriate access and load only the required image size.

lessons.title: Match a Context to its owner
lessons.explanation: A Context provides access to resources and system services. An Activity context also carries screen configuration and theme. Holding that context holds its Activity as long as the reference remains reachable. A process-wide object can outlive many successive Activity instances.
lessons.example: Rotate a themed editor twice. The screen instances are A, B and C. A singleton that stores A as its listener can keep A and its view tree reachable after C appears. Remove the listener when its owner stops observing. Use an application context for a process-wide dependency when it meets the API’s needs.
lessons.exercise: Should a themed dialog use the application context just to avoid a leak?
lessons.answer: Use the active screen’s context for the dialog and bound the dialog’s lifetime to that screen. Correct ownership solves the leak while preserving window and theme information.

lessons.title: Distinguish a task from a process
lessons.explanation: A task is a navigation history of activities. With ordinary launch behavior, starting a new activity adds an entry and Back removes the top activity. The system can preserve task information while reclaiming the app process. The current object instances and the navigation history have different lifetimes.
lessons.example: Open List, Detail and Edit. Back from Edit normally exposes Detail. Reopening a previously backgrounded task may recreate Detail if its original process died. Persist the record and retain a small ID for restoration.
lessons.exercise: If Back reveals Detail, does that prove the same Detail object survived?
lessons.answer: No. Compare navigation identity with object lifetime. A recreated Detail can render the same stored note using restored arguments.
lessons.sourceTitle: Android · Tasks and the back stack

lessons.title: Follow a touch from parent to child
lessons.explanation: A window hosts a hierarchy of views. Once a gesture reaches that hierarchy, a parent ViewGroup can examine it, delegate to a child or intercept later movement. A child that had the gesture must handle cancellation when a parent takes it over.
lessons.example: A button receives DOWN inside a scrolling list. Motion later crosses the parent’s scrolling threshold. The parent intercepts, the child receives CANCEL and the parent handles the scroll. A button that commits on DOWN would have fired during an intended scroll.
lessons.exercise: How would you test a row that accidentally opens while the list moves?
lessons.answer: Record DOWN, MOVE, CANCEL and UP at parent and child. Compare a short tap with a drag crossing the threshold and make activation follow a completed click.
lessons.sourceTitle: Android · Manage touch events in a ViewGroup

lessons.title: Choose a service by its execution contract
lessons.explanation: A Service is an Android component with a lifecycle. By default its callbacks run on the app’s main thread. A started service receives commands; a bound service exposes an interface to clients. A foreground service represents ongoing user-visible work and is subject to launch and type restrictions.
lessons.example: A playback service receives a play command. Its notification makes playback visible; decoding must still run on appropriate execution resources. An expensive synchronous decode in onStartCommand delays other main-thread callbacks.
lessons.exercise: Which component would you choose for an eventual upload that may resume tomorrow?
lessons.answer: A persistent scheduler such as WorkManager suits deferrable work. A foreground playback service meets a different user-visible requirement.

lessons.title: Finish a broadcast before its execution window closes
lessons.explanation: A broadcast delivers a short-lived event to a receiver. Once onReceive returns, an app with no other active component may lose its execution priority. An unmanaged thread started from the callback therefore has no durable lifetime guarantee.
lessons.example: A receiver learns that a local export needs indexing. It records or enqueues uniquely identifiable work and returns. The worker reads the stored input later. goAsync provides only a bounded extension for finishing a broadcast.
lessons.exercise: The same hint arrives twice. What should the indexing worker read?
lessons.answer: Use a durable export identity or current index version and make repeat execution converge to the same result. A broadcast count is a poor substitute for the actual work record.

lessons.title: Give another component a bounded PendingIntent
lessons.explanation: A PendingIntent is a system-maintained token for a specified operation under its creator’s identity. Construct it with an explicit destination and use immutability when the recipient has no need to fill in fields. Equality for matching tokens does not use Intent extras alone.
lessons.example: Two notification actions open note 17 and note 29. If both use the same request code and equal matching Intent fields, different extras alone can select the same token. Give the actions distinct request codes or distinct data URIs.
lessons.exercise: Notification 17 opens note 29 after the second notification arrives. What do you inspect first?
lessons.answer: Compare the operation type, creator, request code, matching Intent fields and update flags. Verify the target checks current authorization when opened.

lessons.title: Persist before process priority changes
lessons.explanation: Android ranks processes partly by their most important active component. A process hosting the visible interaction is typically more important than a cached process. Memory pressure can reclaim cached processes without delivering a final callback in which to save data.
lessons.example: A user saves a draft and backgrounds the app. If the only copy lives in a singleton, reclaiming the cached process removes it. Commit the draft when the edit is accepted; rebuild the screen from an ID after process recreation.
lessons.exercise: Does restoring a navigation screen prove that cached bytes or an unfinished thread survived?
lessons.answer: No. Read the persisted draft and a durable work record. Test with process recreation separately from ordinary rotation.

lessons.title: Separate device idle from app usage restrictions
lessons.explanation: Doze changes the device’s treatment of background network and scheduled work during idle periods. App Standby Buckets classify an individual app by usage and affect its resource opportunities. A delayed job can reflect either policy as well as its own constraints.
lessons.example: An unused news app requests a refresh while an unplugged phone rests with its screen off. Its job can wait even though the stored job record is correct. Inspect device idle state, the app’s bucket, job constraints and actual execution times.
lessons.exercise: Can a periodically requested refresh promise that data is exactly fifteen minutes old at every screen open?
lessons.answer: No. Persist the last successful fetch time, display its age, and define what opening the screen should do if the refresh is overdue.

lessons.title: Schedule around Doze maintenance windows
lessons.explanation: During device idle, Android defers categories of background CPU and network work. Maintenance windows temporarily allow deferred work. A pending operation can be correctly recorded on disk while its first opportunity to contact the server is still in the future.
lessons.example: At 23:00 a device enters idle with a deferred notes upload. The service receives nothing at 23:05. When an allowed window opens, the worker can attempt the upload if its own constraints are also satisfied. Inspect both scheduling and network outcomes before diagnosing a lost edit.
lessons.exercise: A user opens the app before the worker has run. What should their notes screen show?
lessons.answer: Render the local saved edit and its pending state. A background scheduling delay should not erase a draft or falsely mark it synchronized.
lessons.sourceTitle: Android · Optimize for Doze and App Standby

lessons.title: Resume persistent work without repeating its effect
lessons.explanation: WorkManager persists a request and waits for its constraints. The worker may be stopped or run again. A stable work name can coordinate local scheduling; the remote write still needs an identity or a repeat-safe operation.
lessons.example: Persist upload 81. The worker sends it, the server accepts it and the phone stops before recording success. On a later run, the worker resends upload 81. A server that records that identity can return the original result.
lessons.exercise: Would a brand-new server-side upload ID on every worker attempt be safe?
lessons.answer: It could create duplicates. Keep the operation identity with the input, retry transient failure with backoff and mark completion after recovering the outcome.

lessons.title: Trace suspension and dispatch separately
lessons.explanation: A coroutine can suspend by retaining the state needed to continue later. Its thread is then available for other work. A dispatcher chooses where runnable continuations execute. Declaring a function suspend provides no automatic background thread for blocking code.
lessons.example: On Main, delay(100) suspends without holding the main thread for 100 ms. Thread.sleep(100) blocks that thread. Use withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around a blocking file operation and return the result to the caller’s context.
lessons.exercise: A function marked suspend directly parses a large JSON string on Main. Why can scrolling still pause?
lessons.answer: The CPU work runs on the current dispatcher until it suspends or changes context. Move substantial CPU work to an appropriate dispatcher and measure the cost.

lessons.title: Make cancellation observable
lessons.explanation: A coroutine Job expresses a lifetime. Cancelling its owner signals children, but arbitrary running code must reach a cancellation check or a cancellable suspension point. Resource cleanup belongs in a finally block or another construct that runs on exit.
lessons.example: A query changes from ca to cat. Cancel work for ca. A suspending delay observes cancellation promptly; a long CPU loop can check ensureActive between chunks. Also prevent an older result from overwriting the currently requested query.
lessons.exercise: Why can catching every exception and returning a fallback cause a stale result?
lessons.answer: The catch may swallow CancellationException and turn cancelled work into successful output. Propagate cancellation and handle the actual recoverable errors separately.

lessons.title: Decide who starts the producer
lessons.explanation: A cold flow begins its producer for each collection. A shared hot stream has a producer whose lifetime is controlled separately. StateFlow carries the latest state and can conflate successive equal values or let slow collectors skip intermediate states.
lessons.example: Two screens collect flow { emit(loadNotes()) }. The load can run twice. Sharing it with stateIn in a suitable owner scope can give both collectors the same latest list; the chosen sharing policy controls when upstream runs.
lessons.exercise: A payment history must retain every confirmed payment. Is a StateFlow of the latest payment enough?
lessons.answer: Store every payment in a durable collection and expose the latest view of that collection as state. A latest-value stream alone cannot replay every historical transition.

lessons.title: Spend one display interval
lessons.explanation: A frame callback coordinates work with display timing. UI work records or updates drawing commands, rendering work is submitted and the GPU processes it before display composition. CPU and GPU work can overlap across frames, so adding all thread durations does not by itself predict presentation.
lessons.example: At 120 Hz the interval is about 8.33 ms. A 12 ms main-thread layout beginning at the frame opportunity already exceeds one interval even if GPU work is cheap. Inspect the trace to locate the missed deadline.
lessons.exercise: If profiling shows 3 ms of GPU activity for that frame, would lowering shader cost alone fix the 12 ms layout?
lessons.answer: It would leave the identified main-thread cost. Inspect layout and scheduling first, then compare actual presentation deadlines after the change.

lessons.title: Read state in the phase that needs it
lessons.explanation: Compose tracks state reads in composition, layout and drawing. A changed value can restart work from the phase that consumed it. Composition describes nodes, layout measures and places them, and drawing produces pixels.
lessons.example: A background color read inside a draw lambda can invalidate drawing without needing to measure text again. A new text string consumed during composition may change its size and require layout. Inspect where the state value is actually read.
lessons.exercise: A drag changes only placement. What experiment would distinguish composition work from placement work?
lessons.answer: Compare reading position while constructing the modifier with reading it inside a placement lambda. Keep the gesture constant and inspect recomposition counts plus frame timing.

lessons.title: Separate garbage from a leak
lessons.explanation: The managed collector can reclaim objects that no longer have a path from a root. Short-lived allocations can still raise collection frequency. A leaked Activity is reachable even though the product no longer needs it, so repeated collections cannot solve that retention.
lessons.example: Repeated screen rotations create five old editor instances. A heap dump shows a singleton listener registry pointing to all five. Remove registrations on disposal, repeat the rotations and compare the retaining paths and instance counts.
lessons.exercise: What if old editors disappear but allocation rate remains high during drawing?
lessons.answer: That suggests churn on the drawing path, a different mechanism. Record allocations during the same gesture to find objects recreated per frame.
lessons.sourceTitle: Android Studio · Capture a heap dump

lessons.title: Build a dependency graph with explicit lifetimes
lessons.explanation: Constructor injection exposes the objects a class needs. Dagger constructs a graph using generated code; Hilt supplies Android-aware components and scopes on top of Dagger. The scope determines which consumers reuse an instance within that component.
lessons.example: A repository needs a database and a network client. Keep those dependencies in a process-level graph when their lifetimes require it. Create an editor presenter per screen so it can release screen state on destruction.
lessons.exercise: Can a singleton repository safely retain an Activity supplied by a screen component?
lessons.answer: Its longer lifetime would retain a short-lived screen. Pass the needed data or an appropriate process-scoped dependency and leave screen-specific behavior with its owner.

lessons.title: Read a Koin definition as a construction rule
lessons.explanation: Koin resolves definitions from a running container. A single definition reuses an instance within its container lifetime; a factory constructs a fresh value per resolution. A scope can tie an object to a shorter-lived context. Validate that required bindings exist for the production composition.
lessons.example: Two requests for a single database receive the same defined instance. Two requests for a factory editor receive distinct editors. Storing a factory-created editor in a singleton can still extend its actual lifetime.
lessons.exercise: A unit test needs an in-memory repository while the app uses disk. Where should the choice live?
lessons.answer: Bind the implementation at composition or test setup. Keep the consumer’s constructor dependent on the repository contract so its behavior can be exercised independently.

lessons.title: Trace Retrofit down to OkHttp
lessons.explanation: Retrofit maps a declared service method and annotations to an HTTP request and uses converters for supported body types. With an OkHttp-backed client, connection selection, network exchange and interceptors belong to the HTTP layer. Parsing application data and deciding how the UI handles failure are separate boundaries.
lessons.example: A GET method requests notes/17. The server returns HTTP 200 with malformed JSON. The transport received a successful HTTP response, yet the converter can fail before the repository gets a Note. Record the status and the conversion failure separately.
lessons.exercise: If the network times out after a reservation write, would automatically repeating every failed Retrofit call be safe?
lessons.answer: Recover the operation using a stable request identity and a defined server contract. A timeout does not establish whether the server committed the first attempt.

lessons.title: Follow one logical call through OkHttp
lessons.explanation: An OkHttp client owns resources such as a connection pool. Reusing a client allows compatible connections to be reused rather than paying setup for each request. A call can include multiple exchanges, for example when following a redirect. Closing a response body releases its resources.
lessons.example: Two small requests target the same HTTPS origin. The first establishes a connection; the second may use that still-healthy connection. A server close or incompatible route can force a new connection. Measure connection events rather than assuming that an identical URL proves reuse.
lessons.exercise: A chart counts two network exchanges for one app request after a redirect. Does that prove the user tapped twice?
lessons.answer: No. Record the logical call identity and its individual exchanges. Compare original destination, redirect response and final destination before interpreting the count.

lessons.title: Observe a Room query over SQLite
lessons.explanation: Room validates supported annotated SQL and generates DAO plumbing. SQLite still executes the transaction. An observable query can rerun when a table it depends on is invalidated. Schema design, indexes and transaction boundaries still determine work and consistency.
lessons.example: A DAO updates a note title and inserts its pending sync row. Put both statements inside one transaction. A process stop after commit leaves both; a failure before commit leaves neither. The UI observes the resulting local note table.
lessons.exercise: The note is visible after restart but no sync work exists. Which boundary should you inspect?
lessons.answer: Look for separate commits or an independently enqueued in-memory action. Persisting the pending intention with the note makes reconstruction possible.

lessons.title: Measure release code after R8 optimization
lessons.explanation: R8 can shrink unreachable code, optimize bytecode and rename classes or members. Code reached indirectly by reflection may require narrow keep rules. Startup also depends on actual initialization work and compilation, so reducing package size alone cannot establish a faster first frame.
lessons.example: A release build fails to construct a class looked up by name although debug works. Reproduce with the optimized variant, identify the reflective entry point and apply the smallest rule or library-supported declaration that preserves the required contract.
lessons.exercise: After the fix, how would you test the claim that startup improved?
lessons.answer: Benchmark equivalent release variants on the same device and startup mode. Compare first-display measurements and a trace, while holding compilation state and initial data constant.
lessons.sourceTitle: Android · Enable app optimization with R8

title: Inside AOSP: follow a platform service

lessons.title: Read a service declaration from boot to process
lessons.explanation: Android Open Source Project (AOSP) includes init, the first user-space process. Init reads configuration files ending in .rc. A service declaration names a program and its options. An action connects a trigger, such as a property changing value, to commands. To explain why a program appeared, find both its declaration and the action or class start that launched it.
lessons.example: Read this miniature configuration as two stanzas. The first starts with “service fieldlog /vendor/bin/fieldlog” and contains the option “disabled”. The second starts with “on property:vendor.fieldlog.enabled=1” and contains the command “start fieldlog”. The program can be installed throughout boot. The disabled option leaves it out of the ordinary class start, and the explicit start requests it when the action runs.
lessons.exercise: On an Android emulator with adb connected, run adb shell getprop init.svc.zygote. Record the result and the emulator build. If it says running, can you conclude that the launcher has already drawn its first frame?
lessons.answer: Running identifies init's observed service state. The launcher can still be starting. Frame presentation needs a separate observation on the launcher or display timeline. If the property is empty, list the available init.svc properties with adb shell getprop and locate a service declared by that build before drawing a conclusion.
lessons.sourceTitle: AOSP · Android init language and service states

lessons.title: Locate a failing call across the hardware boundary
lessons.explanation: A hardware abstraction layer (HAL) gives platform code an interface to a device-specific implementation. For a binderized HAL, client and implementation live in separate processes. The service registers an instance so a client can find it. AIDL, the Android Interface Definition Language, specifies calls and data across that boundary. A service can start successfully and still return an error when it tries to use the hardware.
lessons.example: Consider a camera request on a build with a binderized camera provider. The app reaches the framework camera service. Its provider lookup succeeds. The provider receives an open request and reports that the device is unavailable. These observations locate the failure after lookup. The device might be occupied, disconnected or in another implementation-defined failure state. A registered instance alone cannot distinguish those explanations.
lessons.exercise: Two traces show the same app error. Trace A ends with provider lookup unsuccessful. Trace B contains provider entry, then a failed device operation. For each trace, choose the first boundary to inspect and predict one observation that would move your investigation elsewhere.
lessons.answer: For A, compare the requested interface and instance with the provider registered on this build. A successful lookup for that exact instance during the failing request moves the investigation past discovery. For B, correlate the provider operation with device state and the request timestamp. A successful device operation followed by a failed reply moves the investigation toward the return path.

lessons.title: Decide whether a framework update fits a vendor image
lessons.explanation: Android can update its framework and device-specific implementation on different schedules. The vendor interface (VINTF) records the contract between them. A manifest describes capabilities a side provides. A compatibility matrix lists what the other side requires. Check both directions when evaluating an image pair. Passing this comparison establishes compatibility of the declarations; live behavior still needs a device test.
lessons.example: Use a simplified contract with exact instance names. The device manifest provides temperature/default. The candidate framework requires temperature/default and fan/default. In the other direction the device requires a diagnostics service that the framework does provide. The first direction fails because fan/default is missing. A successful temperature reading on the old build tells us nothing about this new requirement.
lessons.exercise: An engineer adds fan/default to the manifest without shipping its implementation. Predict what a static comparison using only these declarations could accept. Design a runtime check that would expose the remaining gap.
lessons.answer: The names in the simplified comparison now match. Boot the intended framework and vendor pair on the target device, resolve the named instance and issue a representative supported operation. Record the returned value or failure and a timestamp. Real VINTF matching also considers properties such as interface versions and the applicable matrix level.
lessons.sourceTitle: AOSP · VINTF manifests and compatibility matrices

lessons.title: Account for memory shared by two processes
lessons.explanation: Linux exposes a process's memory mappings under /proc. Resident set size (RSS) counts pages belonging to a mapping that are present in physical memory. Adding RSS across processes can count the same physical page several times. Proportional set size (PSS) apportions the cost of shared pages between their mappings. This matters on Android, where several processes may use the same code pages.
lessons.example: Suppose A and B each have 12 MiB of private resident pages and both map the same 8 MiB of resident code exactly once. Each reports 20 MiB RSS and 16 MiB PSS for those pages. The two together occupy 32 MiB. On Linux with smaps_rollup enabled, run grep -E '^(Rss|Pss):' /proc/self/smaps_rollup. The reported process is grep itself because grep opens the file.
lessons.exercise: B exits while A keeps its mappings, with no eviction or allocation. Predict A's RSS and PSS. Would the PSS change by itself justify filing an app memory leak?
lessons.answer: A's RSS stays at 20 MiB. Its PSS rises to 20 MiB because the eight shared MiB are now entirely attributed to A. To investigate a leak, repeat a bounded operation and look for growth in retained allocations or private memory under comparable conditions. Record other processes that join or leave during the measurement.
lessons.sourceTitle: Linux kernel · Process memory mappings and proportional set size

lessons.title: Recognize a CPU budget in a trace
lessons.explanation: A Linux control group groups processes for accounting and resource control. With the cgroup v2 CPU controller, cpu.max gives a CPU-time allowance and its replenishment period, in microseconds. Threads share that allowance. On several cores, two runnable threads can use it twice as fast in elapsed time. Exhaustion can leave ready work waiting while the host has spare CPU.
lessons.example: For a group with cpu.max set to 50000 100000, the allowance is 50 ms each 100 ms. Assume a fresh period, two continuously running threads on separate cores, no burst allowance and no tighter ancestor limit. They can consume the group's 50 ms in about 25 ms of wall time. Read cpu.stat before and after a slow interval to compare nr_periods and nr_throttled.
lessons.exercise: In one second the host averaged 35% CPU. The group's nr_periods advanced by 10 and nr_throttled by 9. A request took 220 ms. Which explanation is supported? Which measurement would test the specific request?
lessons.answer: The group hit its CPU limit in nine periods. A host average hides that local constraint. The counters cover the whole group, so attributing all 220 ms to throttling is unwarranted. Correlate the request interval with scheduling evidence for its worker. In a controlled repeat, keep work constant and change the CPU allowance, then compare throttling and request latency.
lessons.sourceTitle: Linux kernel · Control group v2 CPU interface

lessons.title: Measure time lost to memory pressure
lessons.explanation: Capacity and delay answer different questions. Linux pressure stall information (PSI) measures time when work stalls on a resource. For memory, some counts time with at least one task stalled, and full counts time when every non-idle task in the measured group is stalled together. The total field accumulates microseconds. Taking two readings gives a measurement for the exact interval you studied.
lessons.example: On a Linux host with PSI enabled, read cat /proc/pressure/memory before and after a timed action. In this example the interval is 5.00 seconds. The some total rises from 8,000,000 to 8,750,000 and full rises by 100,000. Some pressure occupied 15% of the interval. Full pressure occupied 2%. Full is already included in some.
lessons.exercise: A UI pause lasted 300 ms inside that interval. What can the two percentages establish about the pause? How could you distinguish pressure in the app's workload from an unrelated batch job?
lessons.answer: They establish that memory stalls occurred somewhere within the measured host and window. The individual pause still needs attribution. If the app runs in an identifiable cgroup v2 group with PSI, sample its memory.pressure and the host counters over the same action. Correlate an app thread trace with the stalls, then repeat with the batch workload absent. A pressure total can increase even if the UI thread was runnable throughout.
